method.title: Hear it. Understand it. Use it.
method.subtitle: Three steps, repeated until the words come out without you assembling them first.
method.s1Body: Every phrase starts as sound, not spelling. You listen first, replay as often as you like, and read it in Latin letters — no Arabic script required. Until the teacher's recordings are in, a computer voice stands in, and says so.
method.s2Body: Then the meaning: what it says literally, what it actually means, and when a Lebanese person would say it rather than the textbook version.
method.s3Title: Use it in a real conversation
method.s3Body: Finally you answer with it — choosing the natural reply, rebuilding the sentence, and repeating it across days until it's yours.
method.note: Situations, not word lists. You learn a phrase inside the conversation it belongs to, and meet it again a few days later when it's about to slip.

about.title: Born in Beirut. Teaching the Lebanon you won't find in a textbook.
about.p1: I grew up hearing five conversations at once around the same table — that's the Lebanese I teach. Whether you're calling your teta every Sunday, marrying into a Lebanese family, or finally booking that trip to Beirut, I'll get you talking, fast.
about.p2: Every lesson comes from real life: airport small talk, ordering man2ushe, arguing about who pays the bill.
about.note: Everything on this site is free — the lessons, the practice, all seven games. A class is the same thing, with someone listening and correcting you.
about.introBody: A few seconds of Lebanese, at the speed people actually speak it.
about.valueApproachBody: Situations first. You get the phrases a moment actually needs — a greeting, an order, a phone call — and use them out loud before you analyse them.
about.valueDialectBody: What you learn here is the dialect people speak day to day. Where the textbook version differs, I tell you which one to say and which one to only recognise.
about.valuePronunciationBody: Every phrase has a Latin transliteration built for the sounds English doesn't have, and recordings in my own voice are being added. In a class, you say it back and get corrected on the spot.
about.valueClassBody: You speak, I listen and correct, and we work through the situations you actually need. Bring what you didn't understand this week and we start there.
about.valueWhoBody: Complete beginners, heritage speakers who understand more than they say, and anyone who has done the free units and wants someone listening.
about.testimonialsPending: Real student quotes are on the way. Nothing invented goes here.

items.q: Do I need to read Arabic?
items.a: No. Every phrase on this site is written in Latin letters as well as Arabic script. Recordings in the teacher's voice are being added; until a phrase has one, the site says so. You can do the whole course without reading a word of Arabic.

No. Hkeeli teaches spoken Lebanese — the dialect people actually use with each other. Modern Standard Arabic is the written and broadcast language; it is not what you'll hear at a Lebanese dinner table.

items.q: Will I learn the Arabic alphabet?
items.a: Not as a goal here. The Arabic script sits next to every phrase, so you'll start recognising words if you want to — but the lessons, the games and the audio all work from transliteration.

items.q: Is this suitable for complete beginners?
items.a: Yes. Unit 1 starts at hello, and the Start Here questions will send you straight to it if you've never learned any Arabic.

items.q: What variety of Lebanese is taught?
items.a: Everyday spoken Lebanese, taught by a native speaker who grew up with it in Beirut. Where a phrase is casual, polite, affectionate or family-only, the lesson says so.

Classes are one-to-one, or a small group if you'd rather learn with someone you know. Send the booking form and you'll get a reply by email to agree a time; length, price and trial details are confirmed there.
Try the free mini-lesson on the home page. If you'd rather be pointed somewhere specific, answer the three questions on Start Here and you'll get one lesson or activity to begin with.

cafe.setting: You duck into a café off Hamra street. The man behind the counter looks up.

cafe.beat2: One phrase does most of the work here. Learn it properly.

teta.title: Teta on the Phone
teta.setting: The phone rings twice in Beirut and she picks up. You have about two minutes before she switches to English to help you.

teta.beat1: The words that make a grandmother light up.
teta.beat2: One phrase to get right. She'll hear the difference.
teta.beat3: She's talking. Catch what she said.
teta.beat4: Your turn — and don't switch to English.
teta.beat5: Now tell her yourself, word by word.
teta.beat6: The whole call, from “alo”. Put it back in order.

bridge.note: Practice here stays free. The lesson is the part with a person in it.
bridge.strongBody: Recognising a phrase and saying it to someone who answers back are two different skills. The second one needs a person on the other end — which is the whole of what a lesson is.
bridge.mixedBody: The gaps are the useful part. Working out why a phrase isn't landing yet is a teacher's job, and it's the one thing a website can't do for you.
bridge.earlyTitle: Early days — which is the point.
bridge.earlyBody: None of this is meant to be obvious yet. An hour with someone who can hear where you are going wrong moves faster than a week of tapping.
bridge.neutralBody: Reviewing on your own keeps phrases alive. Using them on someone is what turns them into speech.
bridge.sceneTitle: That was a conversation with a website.
bridge.sceneBody: The next one could be with a person who answers something you didn't expect — and can tell you why your version came out differently.

encounter.title: At the café

p.arrive: A table in the shade is free.
p.order: Order your coffee. How do you like it?
p.thanks: He sets it down. What do you say?
p.bill: You're ready to go. Ask for the bill.
p.bye: You've paid. Say goodbye as you leave.

n.arrive: Late afternoon in the courtyard. The waiter is standing by the door.
n.sit: You sit down. The waiter is on his way over.
n.waiter: He comes over to your table.
n.note: You hand him the menu. He writes your order on his pad.
n.coffee: He brings your coffee on a tray.
n.manoushe: A minute later, a manoushe, still warm.
n.enough: He gives a little nod and leaves you to your coffee.
n.bill: He brings the bill on a saucer and takes your order slip.
n.pay: You leave the money on the saucer.

h.order: The menu lists coffee by sugar: wasat is medium-sweet, 3al ri7a has barely any sugar, sada has none. Coffee is 2ahwe — the 2 is a catch in the throat, where a q would be in written Arabic.
h.thanks: He said "here you are… enjoy it". Thank him — shukran, or the warmer Allah ykhallik.
h.more: shi tene? means "anything else?" You can add a zaatar manoushe, or say that's enough.
h.bill: el 7seb is the bill; law sama7t is "if you please". Or just ask how much it comes to.
h.bye: b khatrak is said by the person who is leaving — that's you.

w.notLeaving: That's what you say when you're leaving — you've only just got your coffee.
w.welcome: That's how you answer a thank-you. You want the bill.
w.hello: That's hello. You're on your way out.
